name: Falam Chin (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired bookkeeping code (flm split 2007 into cfm + rnl); no language-specific sources

new_statements.quote: Both stress and intonation are meaningful in their context but they are not contrastive. One common stress pattern in Falam is that diphthongs and contrastively long vowels are stressed [...] A nominalized word with two syllables always stresses the second syllable [...] It is proposed that Falam stress pattern always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word, or even in a final word of connected speech [pp. 59-60]. [...] Stress patterns fall generally upon the second syllable of a compound word consisting of two syllables, and if the word contains more than two syllables, the stress will fall on the last syllable of the word. Being a tonal language, tone is the most fundamental contrastive element in the suprasegmental phonology of Falam. [p. 94]
new_statements.citation: Khar Thuan (2008) A Phonological Description of Falam. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai.
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (138 pp., text; the PDF's metadata dated 2008-02-28, Payap thesis). Quote verified verbatim with extracted text: p.73 (printed 59) sec. 4.2 'Stress' has 'Both stress and intonation are meaningful in their context but they are not contrastive. One common stress pattern in Falam is that diphthongs and contrastively long vowels are stressed ( ˌ is used for stress marker) as in (41)'; p.74 (printed 60) has 'A nominalized word with two syllables always stresses the second syllable as in (42)' [d̪uʔ²¹ˌnaak⁵² 'love' etc.] and 'It is proposed that Falam stress pattern always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word, or even in a final word of connected speech…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Falam Chin is a four-tone language in which stress is non-contrastive; word stress falls on the final syllable of di- and trisyllabic words (second syllable of two-syllable compounds and of verb+nominalizer forms such as duʔ²¹ˌnaak⁵² 'love'), with heavy nuclei (diphthongs, long vowels) described as stressed; native-speaker auditory description, no instrumental stress measurements.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; author notes stress is 'hard to distinguish' from intonation, and separately describes a prefixed /a/ before nouns/adjectives used 'to mark the prominence of the words' (p. 60), which is a morphological emphasis device rather than a stress-placement exception.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic/trisyllabic words, compounds, nominalizations), extended by the author to the final word of connected speech (phrase-final prominence); examples are citation forms with tone numbers and a stress mark on the final syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: fala1245 is Glottolog's bookkeeping ('Retired') entry for the withdrawn ISO 639-3 code [flm] 'Falam Chin', which CR 2006-023 (downloaded, read) split on 2007-07-18 into [cfm] Chin, Falam (Glottolog fala1243) and [rnl] Ranglong. It denotes no language of its own, and under the our rule that a retired code does not make a separate language it must not receive its own catalog row. The first-hand stress statement quoted here (Khar Thuan 2008) describes Falam as spoken in and around Falam town, Chin State -- the Laizo-based lingua franca, author a native speaker, data recorded in Falam Jan-Mar 2006 -- i.e. Falam Chin proper = fala1243 [cfm]; Yip 2004 and Osburne 1975 describe the Zahao/Zahau dialect of the same language. Recommendation: reclassify this result (files in, see) to fala1243, which is a separate our source list key carrying exactly these Glottolog refs and whose earlier scan was the named source could not be reached; as a fala1243 entry the Khar Thuan quote would be a valid first-hand catalog candidate. Nothing was found or is known to me for the Ranglong [rnl] half of the split.

One common stress pattern in Falam is that diphthongs and contrastively long vowels are stressed [...] A nominalized word with two syllables always stresses the second syllable [...] It is proposed that Falam stress pattern always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word, or even in a final word of connected speech [pp. 59-60]. sources.note: Sec. 4.2 'Stress' (pp. 59-60) and ch. 7 (p. 94): Falam is tonal (4 tones); stress is not contrastive; diphthongs/long vowels attract stress; nominalized disyllables stress the 2nd syllable; stress 'always occurs in the last syllable of disyllabic word or trisyllabic word' -- i.e. word-final stress.
